title: Yakuza: A 400-Year History of the Japanese Underworld
gist: Elizabeth Economy's review of Andrew Rankin's history of the Yakuza argues the group's 400-year survival rested on its usefulness to economic and political elites, and its marginalization since the 1980s followed the state's growing capacity and shifting needs.

insights.claim: Japan's Yakuza have survived for roughly 400 years chiefly because they were useful to economic and political elites, not because of criminal strength alone.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Organized crime that serves elites persists; when the state internalizes those functions, such groups decline.
insights.quote: He argues convincingly that the most important factor in the Yakuza’s longevity has been its usefulness to economic and political elites.

insights.claim: Beyond gambling dens, brothels and extortion, Yakuza groups performed quasi-public functions: helping police recover stolen goods, running municipal rat-eradication campaigns, staffing local fire brigades, and deterring blackmailers for businesses.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Illustrates how criminal organizations embed in gaps left by weak state capacity.
insights.locator: Across centuries, members of criminal groups

insights.claim: The Japanese national government enlisted the Yakuza to suppress labor unrest and left-wing political movements, such as those in the early 1900s.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: State use of criminal proxies against political opponents is a recurring pattern in industrializing states.

insights.claim: Since the 1980s the Yakuza's influence has steadily diminished because of international concern about their role in Japanese business deals and the Japanese government's expanding capabilities.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Organized-crime exposure shrinks as state capacity and international scrutiny of corporate dealings rise.

insights.claim: A national fire service, democratization, globalization and stronger anti-organized-crime laws pushed the Yakuza from the center of Japanese public life to its margins, where members blend into mainstream society while still working underground as fixers and extortionists.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Residual risk persists in Japanese corporate dealings even as the Yakuza's visible role fades.
insights.locator: The creation of a national fire service
